text: Meet Ramesh, an ordinary man with an exhausting life. All he wants after a long day is to come home and sleep. But next door, the drilling never stops. His bed shakes, his walls tremble, and there are vibrations all over his room. His nights turn sleepless. So what he does is record it, records it every tremor, every night. He takes government to court, but his evidence is tampered with. The records are rewritten, and officially, there was no construction. Instead of justice, Ramesh is handed with a def-defamation case. That very night, he lies awake again. The bed shakes, but this time it isn't the construction. It's an earthquake. By morning, rescuers pull survivors from rubble one by one, but Ramesh is still trapped. No one knows where he is. What if the vibrations we ignore today could save lives tomorrow? So we introduce you TremorMesh. Sense, map, and prove every tremor because every tremor tells a story. TremorMesh for Ramesh. Every tremor matters. And this Ramesh is a story, but this... these are not. These are real-life cases which happened real... in last year. Real cases, real buildings, Mumbai. Every blow next door travels through ground into old building like Ramesh's. Cracks grow, but nobody keeps an honest record. This is TremorMesh. Every flat keeps one phone on the floor. Together, they record every tremor, and nobody can rewrite that record, not even us. The phone lies still and listens. It reacts only when the floor really shakes. Pick it up, and the reading doesn't count. One phone, one phone actually proves nothing, and one man is easy to dismiss. A tremor only counts when three flats feel it at the same moment. The building committee invites each phone. Every phone gets a public name, and the rules are public too. Each phone signs what it felt, like a signature on a letter. Change one number, and everyone can see it, so there is no evidence tampering or anything. Under the hood, every reading is signed, stored on archive and a public, which is a public blockchain database. Names and rules live on ENS. And after that, for an event, a sealed evidence sits on a SWAMP, and your own browser does the counting, not our servers. Here is the real thing demonstrated at ETHGlobal Mumbai. Four phones, four phones, one table of hundred and forty-one readings. A hundred and thirty-seven were thrown out. One real event got through at twenty-three hundred hours. It was sealed for good. But the night the bed shook, it wasn't a construction. It was an earthquake. When the internet go do- goes down, the same phones become a rescue network. When enough phones feel a strong quake at once, they switch to disaster mode. With no internet, they connect directly over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, thereby forming a mesh. Some phones become hubs linked to many others. Some become connectors, bridging groups, so mes- every message finds a way through. Every link also shows how close two phones are, giving a map of who is near to whom, so it's like relative distance of each other. If a phone goes quiet under the rubble, its last neighbors show rescuers where to look. Here is how our app works with no internet. One phone taps, "I need help," and it hops through a mesh to everyone. It's completely encrypted. The list shows who's safe, who needs help, and who hasn't answered. Bevo- before disaster, a proof no one can rewrite, and after it, a way to find each other. TremorMesh.
